items.content:
Get our
breaking news email
,
free app

daily news podcast
Pauline Hanson
has released a statement this morning
welcoming South Australian senator
Leah Blyth
to her party
.
Blyth is the second high-profile federal defection from the Coalition to One Nation – after
Barnaby Joyce
.
Senator Blyth will be One Nation’s first South Australian Senator and will build on One Nation’s expanding support within the state.
My team and I are delighted to welcome Senator Blyth to sit in the Senate with One Nation.
We are facing at the next election clearly a coalition of the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation, with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. They’re all anti-worker, they’re all extreme … this demonstrates, I think, more disunity in the Liberal party under
Angus Taylor
.

items.title: Social media making it harder for UK parents to raise families, survey finds
items.content:
Poll of parents of young children finds three-quarters think pressure from influencers has increased their anxiety
Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media influencers to be “the perfect parent” is making it harder to raise a family, according to a
survey
.
Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”.

items.title: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress
items.content:
Victims’ commissioner welcomes strengthening of law in England and Wales but calls for measures to tackle convicted stalkers
Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.
Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.
Continue reading...

items.title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling named Waterstones book of the year
items.content:
The word-of-mouth success of the journalist’s investigation into the death of a London teenager is ‘one of the defining features of the literary year’
London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.
The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.

Children who share a bedroom and lack a quiet place to study at home get worse GCSE results than their peers, according to a major report on how poor housing affects education.
The research, carried out by leading academics at University College London for the Sutton Trust, a social mobility charity, urged UK ministers to ensure all young people in rented accommodation have space for a desk.

items.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
items.content:
Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war
Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.
She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.

items.title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses

Beaches close as Los Angeles and La Jolla see all-time high tides and big waves batter landmark pier in Pacifica
Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.
As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets
reported
. The pier, which had once housed a
favorite local cafe
, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the
San Francisco Chronicle reported
, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells
12 times stronger than on an average November day.

items.content:
Explosion heard in Riyadh after 'hostile aerial threat' warning, report says
An explosion was heard in Saudi capital Riyadh on Wednesday, according to an AFP journalist and residents, a day after 11 people were wounded in a Houthi-claimed attack on the city's financial district.
The explosion occurred around midnight local time after authorities issued an alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat", which was lifted shortly after. Residents in northern and eastern Riyadh confirmed hearing the blast, with one saying their house windows "shook violently".

items.title: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
items.content:
US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.
Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "
not certain
that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".
That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

items.title: Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
items.content:
Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 21:13
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman expected to travel to the US next month for G-20 in first trip since start of war
This aerial photograph shows a view of the Riyadh skyline on 23 November 2026
Off
Fresh explosions rocked Riyadh on Wednesday as Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on
Saudi Arabia’s
Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
The Houthis said that both strikes on the ports “resulted in damage” while the Saudi-led coalition acknowledged that a projectile hit the port of Jazan, resulting in minor damage and no casualties.
The port strikes followed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery. Argus Media, which covers commodity markets, said the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal. The Houthis say they bombed Ras Tanura as retaliation for the Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah controlled by the group.
Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and Western officials tell Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side. Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to delivering military support to Saudi Arabia, but with the exception of Syria - which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.
The Crown Prince met
US
Central Command chief admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE
first reported
the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.
The US, Saudi Arabia's top military supplier, however has not publicly committed additional support to the kingdom, although it has troops and advisers inside the country.
Iran tensions simmer
Semafor reported on Wednesday that Mohammed bin Salman will travel to the US next month for the G-20 summit in Miami. Diplomats have speculated for months whether the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia would leave the kingdom amid Houthi strikes and the chances of a new US-Israeli attack on Iran.
'Turn on the weapons spigot': Saudi Arabia asks partners for gear to deter Houthis
Read More »
Tensions between the US and Iran have been simmering for months, with the two sides exchanging blows in the Strait of Hormuz and at some land targets. The US has conducted strikes on Iran’s mainland while Tehran has responded with attacks on US military sites in Kuwait and Bahrain.
Iran said on Wednesday that an oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.
Brent, the international oil benchmark, was up 2.5 percent on Wednesday, trading at $84 per barrel.
The Trump administration says that it is not interested in resuming the war on Iran for now, and instead wants to use economic means to collapse the government, mainly through a blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran has been hit by debilitating inflation, although regional officials who have traveled to the capital have reported busy restaurants and a sense of calm. Fars said on Wednesday that a substantial shipment of dollar banknotes had entered Iran from a neighbouring country.

items.title: Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
items.content:
Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem on Wednesday demanded the immediate release of five men identified as members of the Lebanese movement and accused of forming an armed cell.
Speaking in a televised address broadcast by Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel, Qassem said the men had "done nothing wrong" and "must be released immediately".
Security forces had detained the five earlier this month in a mountainous area in northern Lebanon, a predominantly Christian region far from Hezbollah's main strongholds.
A judge on Wednesday ordered their continued detention pending investigation, a judicial source told AFP.
"We are being patient in order to preserve civil peace, but patience in the face of injustice has limits," Qassem warned, adding the group would "push back against danger" if necessary.

items.title: New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade postponed due to weather
items.content:
Forecasters say high winds on Thursday may spoil the annual march of huge balloons and have moved the parade to Saturday
New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to excessively windy weather and will now be held on Saturday.
Forecasters say an impending storm on Thursday may spoil the street party, which is marked by a march of huge balloons. AccuWeather is forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 km/h) and rain later on Thursday.

items.title: Thirty-one killed in fire after vehicle overturns in Egypt
items.content:
By Enas Alashray and Yomna Ehab
CAIRO, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Thirty-one people were killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned on a major ring road in Egypt, authorities said on Wednesday.
The fire broke out above a tunnel in Giza's Al-Warraq district, the public prosecution said. Preliminary estimates found that 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, had been charred, it said, adding that casualty figures and damage were still being assessed.

items.title: Israeli judges recommend prosecutors drop one bribery case against Netanyahu
items.content:
JERUSALEM, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Israeli judges on Wednesday recommended that prosecutors drop one of three long-running cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsider another alleging he granted favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He denies the charges and has pleaded not guilty. His trial began in 2020 and involves three criminal cases.

items.title: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
items.content:
US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 18:44
The president's abrupt announcement came on the morning of the midterm elections earlier this month
Students carry placards depicting US President Donald Trump and Israel's caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu carrying guns, as they march during a general strike over rising living costs and military spending called by the CGIL trade union, in Milan, Italy, on 20 November 2026 (Claudia Greco/Reuters)
Off
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.
Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "
not certain
that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".
That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.
In May, the Israeli defence ministry said that the two sides had begun formal talks to replace the current memorandum, with discussions focusing on joint investment in research, development and weapons production.
The suggested framework was to move the relationship from aid to a more reciprocal partnership.
The Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan research body that advises the US Congress, further confirmed this in a June report that US and Israeli officials were discussing a possible shift after 2028 away from direct military aid and towards joint programmes.
Israel, a full-scale partner
In July, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives narrowly passed a $1.5 trillion budget for the US Department of War, and the bill included a controversial provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Netanyahu
put it
- turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner.
Future presidents would not be able to simply withdraw from such a project.
Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
Read More »
The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is must-pass legislation, as it is needed to fund all of the Pentagon's operations in the year to come. The Senate will have to consider it soon.
But emboldened by the incoming Democratic majority in January, a dozen Democrats, led by Maryland Senator
Chris Van Hollen
, are
seeking to remove
the provisions related to Section 219, which establishes the "United States–Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative".
The project would identify jointly developed or Israeli-origin technologies for potential integration into US systems; ensure collaborative research initiatives involving government, private sector and academic institutions in both countries protect "sensitive technology"; and ultimately align military efforts with the Department of War that include the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Missile Defense Agency and the United States Space Command, among others.
Huckabee said at the Institute for National Security Studies conference on Tuesday that American lives are saved "every day" because "we pick up intelligence from our partners in Israel".
Military ties continue
On 3 November, Trump said that his administration will not give its yearly military aid to Israel starting next year, because of a prior understanding he made with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Trump added that weapon sales and other forms of military cooperation would continue.
Speaking on Fox News, the president said that the two had agreed months ago to end the military aid since Israel no longer needed it.
Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy
Read More »
“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump said.
“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he added.
Trump said Israel would be able to purchase weapons from the United States and other countries, suggesting that the change would affect the form of assistance rather than bring an end to military ties.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," he said.
The comments came as Republican lawmakers and establishment Democrats running for Congress - as well as hundreds of statewide races - faced growing electoral pressure over support for Israel ahead of the midterm elections.
And indeed, the so-called
blue tsunami
, led by an energised progressive Democratic movement that wants to curb US aid to Israel, washed over Capitol Hill and state legislatures, including several governorships.

نتانياهو يطالب بإنهاء محاكمته بعد توصية قضائية بإسقاط تهمة الرشوة عنه
طالب رئيس حكومة تصريف الأعمال في إسرائيل بنيامين نتانياهو، الأربعاء، بإنهاء محاكمته بتهم الفساد فورا، بعدما أوصى قضاة المحكمة المركزية في القدس بإسقاط تهمة الرشوة الموجهة إليه في إحدى القضايا، وإعادة النظر في أخرى، والتوصل إلى تسوية في الثالثة. ويأتي ذلك في لحظة سياسية فاصلة قد تشهد فقدانه للمنصب والتحصين القضائي، بعد إخفاقه في الانتخابات الشهر الماضي، وتكليف خصمه غادي آيزنكوت بتشكيل الحكومة الجديدة.

items.title: Egypt says 31 dead in Cairo fire after fuel truck overturns
items.content:
A fire erupted in Egyptian capital Cairo on Wednesday killing at least 31 people, the health ministry said, after a fuel truck reportedly overturned on a packed highway.
AFP footage showed a huge fireball and thick black smoke rising above the densely populated capital's Al-Waraq neighbourhood as motorists sounded their horns and scrambled to get away. Surrounding buildings appeared to escape the flames.

items.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts Houthi drone near Jeddah Islamic Port
items.content:
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts Houthi drone near Jeddah Islamic Port
The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday it intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis near Jeddah Islamic Port on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, adding that no civilians were injured by debris from the interception.
The Houthis said they had attacked the port.
Jeddah Islamic Port is a major Saudi maritime gateway on the Red Sea and a key hub for cargo and container traffic.
A picture taken on 1 March 2022 shows a view of cranes and shipping containers at a loading dock of Jeddah's Islamic Seaport on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast (AFP)

items.title: Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
items.content:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
In 2021,
Israeli
police arrested a
Palestinian
man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.
He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.
The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.
Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.
Read more:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
Palestinians released from Israeli prisons are examined by medics at the Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital in Deir el-Balah in the central Gaza Strip on 10 April 2025 (Eyad Baba/AFP)

Controlled blast to dispose of lead azide risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in 100-mile radius
The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material lead azide in
Iowa
on Wednesday morning, despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
The controlled blast, which took place at about 10.00am ET, was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the chemical that was stored at the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people.

items.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
items.content:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged
A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.
The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

items.title: UK moving military planes into hangars amid drone threat: Reports
items.content:
UK moving military planes into hangars amid drone threat: Reports
Britain's air force is moving planes into hangars and hardened shelters overnight to protect them from drone threats, The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday.
The two UK media outlets also revealed plans by the Royal Air Force (RAF) to install anti-drone nets around warplanes that remain exposed.
The Ministry of Defence did not confirm the reports, but in a statement to AFP said it takes "the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and (is) always adapting to counter any potential threats".
The ministry said it was "investing an additional £470 million ($615 million) to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities".
British authorities have regularly issued warnings about the threats posed by Russia and Iran and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies.

items.title: UK politics: Burnham dismisses Badenoch’s criticism over influencer and declines to apologise for ‘vile video’ – as it happened
items.content:
Pair clashed at PMQs over a video shot outside No 10 by TikToker Max Balegde
Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration.
Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to
new research published today
by King’s College University and YouGov.
Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters.
It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity.

items.content:
Wife said to detectives: ‘I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true’
A woman who was allegedly raped and sexually assaulted by men her husband invited to their home after he drugged her told police she could not believe it happened.
In a video interview played to a jury at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, she told detectives: “I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true, and I think you have made a mistake.”

items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
items.content:
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
Yemen's
Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on
Saudi Arabia's
largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, on Wednesday, describing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi strikes that have killed scores of civilians.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the refinery attack caused fires and came in retaliation for the "brutal Saudi aggression against our country, including its targeting of passenger buses and citizens' trucks in the Al-Maqatirah district of Lahij, as well as other crimes in the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates."
The attack in the district of Lahij earlier this week killed at least 26 people.

items.title: The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
items.content:
The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 14:23
A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away in the remote roof of the Sahara has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars
The Tibesti mountains run through northern Chad into southern Libya, and are home to the Tubu people (MEE)
Off
Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis.
A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.
A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara.
These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern
Libya
, northern Niger and northwestern
Sudan
.
And the valleys that surround the town of Miski contain vast deposits of a precious metal that throughout human history has been prized almost above anything else: gold.
The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities.
For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan, then Chadian states.
Now, the Tubu find themselves caught up in a web of warfare and illicit trade that stretches out from Chad into Libya, Sudan and over the sea to the
United Arab Emirates
, from where arms and supplies are flown to proxy armies, militias and paramilitaries.
On 14 October, armed clashes broke out in Miski.
The day after fighting began, the Chadian army’s general staff
accused
Miski’s self-defence committee - a local armed group descended from the Tubu institution of village guardianship - of breaking a peace agreement struck between them and the army last year by attacking the National Brigade for the Control of Mining Activities.
The army gave the Tubu group an ultimatum: lay down your arms at once or be treated as rebels. In response, the committee
accused
the brigade of firing first and of opening new mining fronts in grazing lands, in violation of
the Bardai peace accord
signed last year.
The gold ends up in Dubai…'yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti'
-
Tubu commander
One Tubu commander in Miski told Middle East Eye that last year Chad had exported over $1bn worth of gold and more than 15,000 tonnes of antimony, all sourced from the Tibesti mountains.
Almost all this
gold ends up in the UAE
, in the gold market of Dubai.
“And yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti,” the commander said. “We won’t let this continue.”
Since the armed clashes broke out in October, the Chadian army has moved considerable numbers of troops and armoured vehicles into the Tibesti.
The situation on the ground, according to one Chadian army officer who spoke to MEE, is difficult for government troops. “We are fighting the mines and the mountains in Miski,” he said.
This fighting has not stopped: scores of people have died in the clashes and the Chadian army has conducted multiple drone strikes across the mountain range.
Weapons corridor
Miski’s uprising appears, on the surface, to be a local fight over gold - and in a large part, it is.
But it is unfolding inside a region that has become one of the most consequential, least scrutinised arms corridors in Africa: a route that, according to United Nations investigators and
extensive reporting
from Middle East Eye, has carried weapons, fuel and fighters from the UAE through Libya and Chad to the paramilitary
Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
in Sudan.
How the UAE continued supporting Sudan's RSF through Haftar and Libya
Read More »
These weapons are part of a
network of arms and mercenaries
that spans swathes of north and central Africa, utilised not just in Sudan but by organised criminal groups and armed entities across the Sahel.
Between October 2024 and the end of 2025,
according to a UN Panel of Experts report
, heavy cargo aircraft made 458 flights between military airports in the UAE or the Emirati base at Bosaso in the breakaway Somali region of Puntland and eastern Libya.
Some 239 of these landed at Kufra, a town about 300km from the Sudan border that was
transformed
, in the months before the RSF took el-Fasher in October 2025, into a fortified logistics hub complete with new hangars and scheduled flights.
Separately, as
reported by MEE
and confirmed by UN experts, the UAE was using Amdjarass, in eastern Chad, to land cargo planes.
Senior Egyptian army sources
told MEE
earlier this year that the Emiratis have a military operations room inside Amdjarass airport to coordinate with the RSF.
Just over 100km from the border with Darfur, the vast western region of Sudan controlled by the RSF, Amdjarass is a Zaghawa-dominated town that is the home region of Chad’s president, Mahamat Idriss Deby, and the site of a lavish state infrastructure programme that residents of Tibesti, 1,300km away and without a single paved road or a functioning hospital between them, have started to openly resent.
Abu Dhabi continues to deny supplying the Rapid Support Forces.
Haftar’s expanding footprint
In November 2025, Chad and the UAE-backed Haftar family’s Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), de facto commanded by Khalifa Haftar’s son Saddam,
formed a joint border force
covering roughly 1,050km of shared frontier.
The Haftars are not just in control of eastern Libya:
leaked details
of
US
adviser
Massad Boulos
’s plan to unify Libya propose Saddam Haftar as president of a government that would continue to be led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.
Chad’s government has two reasons to want this partnership, and they reinforce each other.
One is logistical: Chad and Haftar can cement their relationship in the eastern Libyan corridor that carries Emirati arms to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan.
The other is that a joint border force hems in the Tubu, who have supplied the armed resistance to Mahamat Deby’s government and to Haftar’s forces alike.
Jalel Harchaoui, an analyst focusing on Libya and political economy, told Middle East Eye that when the deal was initially struck, the Tubu were not part of the thinking.
The only connection in the remote area - Starlink (MEE)
“It was to ensure better security along the route between Chad and Libya, especially with the passage via Ma’tan as-Sarra in Libya down through Chad to Amdjarass and then on to Darfur,” he said.
This “security problem” included armed groups attacking the convoys headed to Darfur to supply the RSF, Harchaoui said. There was also the need to build further cooperation between Emirati allies who were not natural bedfellows.
“Saddam Haftar and Mahamat Deby don’t get along, so there was a need to please the UAE by doing a joint force. And the agreement was never that the joint force would be pushed to the west, it was really to cover the northeastern corner of Chad,” Harchaoui said.
That changed earlier this year, when Saddam Haftar “ran into trouble” with armed Tubu groups like the Southern Liberation Operations Room (Slor), which is led by Mohamed Wardougou, a Libyan Tubu, and often hides out in northern Niger.
Haftar asked Chad to move forces to the west, arguing correctly, according to Harchaoui, “that Wardougou’s activism served as a shot in the arm for the anti-Deby Chadian group Front for Change and Concord in Chad (Fact) in northern Niger”.
History of revolt
This move played into the Tubu’s long record of rising up against the central governments of Chad, going back to the country’s independence from
France
in 1960.
Their most recent armed revolt, in April 2021, culminated in the
death
on the front line of President Idriss Deby Itno, who had decided at the age of 68 to command his forces in person. His son Mahamat succeeded him.
In Libya too, the Tubu rose against Muammar Gaddafi, and after his fall in 2011, they held sway over vast stretches of southern Libya until 2021, when Haftar’s forces pushed into the areas they had controlled. The containment effort carries a human cost well beyond Tibesti.
In Libya, Tubu communities describe a steady tightening around their citizenship, with human rights researchers
long having flagged
discriminatory practices such as treating the Tubu as second-class citizens and stopping them from obtaining passports and IDs.
'We do not want to be part of a bigger game… We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region'
-
Tubu defence committee member
On 14 October, the same day gunfire broke out in Miski, Libya’s attorney general in Tripoli
said
he was prepared to strip the 28,000 families registered at Murzuq, in the Fezzan region of southwest Libya, of their Libyan nationality, citing alleged forgery.
Because the overwhelming majority of Libya’s Tubu are registered through that one civil registry, the announcement reads as an existential threat: if carried through, most of Libya’s Tubu would become stateless.
On the border between Libya and Niger, Wardougou’s Slor group has fought a running battle with Haftar’s forces, using northern Niger as a rear base. The Slor’s declared aim is to remove Haftar’s men from southern Libya.
In July, photographs circulated online showing Chadian soldiers at Libya’s Wigh airbase, near the Nigerien border - evidence, the group’s leadership says, that Chad is fighting on Haftar’s behalf.
On 20 October, the LAAF
arrested
a former Chadian minister and senior opposition figure, Hassan Soukaya, as he tried to cross from Libya into Niger, and handed him to the Chadian army.
Days later, Niger’s government
publicly accused
the Chadian military, with alleged French support, of carrying out a drone strike on 24 October near the Salvador Pass that killed two civilians. The attack was
reportedly
meant to target Slor positions in Libya, but hit Nigerien territory by accident.
The UAE-Israel desert axis
On 19 October, Israel’s second-ever ambassador to Chad landed in N’Djamena to present her credentials to Deby.
Since taking power after his father’s death in 2021, Deby has made a point of binding Chad ever closer to the UAE and Israel: diplomatic relations with Israel were
restored i
n 2022, and the first Israeli ambassador in more than half a century - since Chad broke off ties in 1972 - was received shortly afterwards. Despite this, in November 2023, Chad
recalled
its ambassador from Israel, citing “the unprecedented tide of deadly violence” inside Gaza.
Chadian alignment with the UAE is not only military. As previously
reported by MEE
, the Emiratis offered Deby “more than a billion dollars” to “flip Chad towards supporting the RSF” after the war in Sudan began, according to former CIA analyst Cameron Hudson.
Senior UAE and regional officials referred to ICC over role in Sudan atrocities
Read More »
That figure now looks like loose change. In May 2025, in Abu Dhabi, Chad unveiled
Chad Connexion 203
0, a $30bn national development strategy to remake the infrastructure of a landlocked country from the ground up.
The UAE was, by a wide margin, its most important bilateral underwriter, securing $20.5bn in total backing and signing 18 contracts of its own worth over $6.2bn.
Among the
headline projects
: an 800-km Etihad rail line to Cameroon’s port of Douala, a
50 MWp solar plant by Global South Utilities
, industrial zones, Abu Dhabi Ports logistics hubs, and critical-mineral exploration permits.
The partnership has tightened Chad’s dependence on the UAE and has become, in effect, the economic lifeline of Deby’s administration. To the west, Chad is already at odds with its neighbour Niger, which has drawn closer to Algeria.
In late October, Algeria
deployed troops
to Niger, the first time it had done this outside its borders since 1973. The move came days after Niger’s military government survived
a coup attempt
on 28 August.
Algeria’s move into Niger, according to the retired Algerian diplomat Amar Belani, is designed to
counter
what he described as “a destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies.”
The current geopolitical shifts, Belani went on, together with all they entail by way of rivalry and intervention by foreign actors, mean that “new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s red lines.”
Borderlands unrest
What is forming, in other words, is not one war but two rival blocs assembling around unrest in the desert borderlands.
Rape, ransom and execution: The road out of Sudan's el-Fasher
Read More »
On one side: the Sudanese Armed Forces (which receives backing from Egypt and Turkey), Niger, Algeria, and the Tubu in Libya and Chad. On the other: the RSF, the Haftars, the UAE, Ethiopia and the Chadian state, with the French leaning towards this camp.
And the local fights and the larger one are no longer separate. A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away deep in the remote mountains of Chad has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars, with a succession contest inside Libya’s eastern military establishment, and a Sahelian realignment redrawing alliances from Algiers to Khartoum.
“We do not want to be part of a bigger game,” one member of the Tubu defence committee in Miski told MEE. “We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region.”
But whether it remains a local counter-insurgency or becomes the spark for something larger will depend less on what happens in the mountains of Tibesti than on decisions being made in Abu Dhabi, Benghazi and Paris.
Sahel
Oscar Rickett
Miski, Chad

items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
items.content:
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 15:56
Yemeni movement says the refinery attack was in retaliation to Saudi strikes, including one that killed at least 26 people earlier this week
This satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery on 25 November 2026 (Planet Labs PBC/Handout via Reuters)
Off
Yemen's
Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on
Saudi Arabia's
largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, on Wednesday, describing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi strikes that have killed scores of civilians.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the refinery attack caused fires and came in retaliation for the "brutal Saudi aggression against our country, including its targeting of passenger buses and citizens' trucks in the Al-Maqatirah district of Lahij, as well as other crimes in the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates."
The attack in the district of Lahij earlier this week killed at least 26 people.
In a follow-up post on X, Saree responded to Saudi threats to retaliate against Yemen's civilian Hodeidah port, which Saudi Arabia has already bombed, by warning that all "enemy Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will be targets".
"We warn employees, workers and those near these ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away, and we call on all shipping companies to remove their ships from those ports immediately," the post added.
Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, which controls the capital Sanaa and much of north and western Yemen, has been firing missiles at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in a spillover from the Israeli-US war on
Iran
.
Riyadh broke the ceasefire, which also included Saudi Arabia, when it bombed Sanaa's international airport on 13 July.
Since then, the Saudi military has struggled to contain the Houthis and their ability to counter Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.
The ongoing attacks are wreaking havoc on the Saudi economy, oil infrastructure and the country's international image.
Airlines have cancelled international flights from the Saudi capital, Riyadh, while previous attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure have disrupted oil supplies.
The attacks have also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship Future Investment Initiative conference.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudis said that air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the country's Eastern Province. They did not deny that the attack had struck the oil refinery there.
Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
Read More »
Satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed large swathes of thick black smoke around the refinery, covering an area spanning around 600 square kilometres.
The Houthis have previously targeted Ras Tanura, which has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, during the conflict.
The refinery forms part of a strategic complex on the kingdom's Gulf coast facing Iran, through which the country exported most of its oil before the Israel-US war on Iran started on 28 February.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has had to send some of its oil through Yanbu on the west coast along the Red Sea, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline and has also faced attacks.
Separately, Houthi spokesman Saree had also said the group had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases.
Saudi civil defence said a strike on Tuesday wounded 11 people at a tower in Riyadh’s financial district. The tallest building in the capital, the tower houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week.
The first, on 19 November, damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence posted an image on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some damage about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact of last week's attack.

“Two groups of hackers accessed Russia’s main statistics database last month and discovered a cache of 11m death certificates that revealed nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022. Among these were 1,000 – the equivalent of a whole regiment – who took their own lives.
The documents show how the majority of soldiers come from poorer areas and ethnic minorities, drawn in by high salaries. There are also recruits from abroad and even those lured to Russia by offers of jobs.

Iran has backed Lebanon's “inherent right to defend its territorial integrity and national sovereignty" and condemned Israeli attacks on the country's south.
“The intensification of the Zionist regime’s aggressive actions against Lebanon – coinciding with the country’s independence commemorations – constitutes a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter and the November 2024 ceasefire agreement,” the Iranian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
“This underscores the stark reality that the Zionist enemy represents the gravest threat to the independence, territorial integrity, security, and stability of Lebanon.”

items.title: Israeli lawmakers advance October 7 inquiry opposed by Netanyahu
items.content:
Israel's new parliament on Wednesday took a first step to set up a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas's unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, a move long opposed by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
On the election campaign trail, centrist prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot had pledged to swiftly establish an independent state commission into the failures that allowed Hamas's attack which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.

items.title: Eastern Libya leader Haftar visits Erdogan in Turkey as ties thaw
items.content:
Khalifa Haftar, leader of the eastern half of divided Libya, met President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Wednesday on his first formal visit to Turkey, the presidency said.
The meeting marks a thaw between the longtime rivals.
Turkey backed the Tripoli-based, UN-recognised government against Haftar's eastern forces during Libya's civil war, but Ankara has in recent years sought to deepen ties with power brokers across the divided country.

items.title: Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib join politicians and legal groups condemning Ulm 5 prosecution
items.content:
Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib join politicians and legal groups condemning Ulm 5 prosecution
Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 13:02
Two letters signed by 26 politicians and 31 legal groups demand the 'immediate release' of defendants in Germany
The 'Ulm Five' from left to right: Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo (supplied)
Off
Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib are among dozens of politicians and legal organisations raising alarm over the prosecution and treatment of pro-
Palestine
activists in
Germany
.
Two letters issued on Wednesday, signed by 26 politicians and 31 legal groups from across the globe, condemned the treatment of five activists who have been held in pretrial detention for over 14 months.
Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo, who are from Germany,
Spain
,
Ireland
and the
UK
, were arrested on 8 September following an alleged break-in at the premises of
Israeli
arms firm Elbit Systems in the southwestern German city of Ulm.
Known as the “Ulm Five”, the group is accused of damaging the building's glass facade and smashing office equipment, including computers, screens and telephones.
In addition to charges of trespass and damage to property, the five are accused of "membership of a criminal organisation", namely Palestine Action Germany, under Section 129 of the German penal code.
The legislation is typically used to target organised crime networks and carries a potential sentence of up to five years in prison.
All the defendants have been held in prolonged pretrial detention, where they report facing restrictive conditions.
Under Section 129, suspects can be held for up to six months before trial, though lawyers say this period has now been significantly extended.
In their letter, the elected officials - including members of the German Bundestag, the European Parliament, the US Congress, the Irish Parliament and other legislatures across Europe and the Americas - called for the activists’ “immediate release”.
They further warned that the implications of their prosecution and treatment extend beyond the five defendants, forming “part of an international effort to discipline opposition to war and to place the interests of arms manufacturers above the rights of peoples and the obligations of international law”.
'Politically inconvenient facts'
Meanwhile, a separate letter signed by 33 legal groups - including the Center for Constitutional Rights, the Punjab Bar Council, European Democratic Lawyers, the American Association of Jurists, the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, the German Association of Democratic Lawyers - warned that the conduct of the trial could constitute a breach of German and international law.
In particular, the letter raises concerns about the courtroom’s security arrangements, which it said obstruct confidential communication between the defendants and their lawyers and could undermine the presumption of justice.
MEE previously
reported
that the trial, which began on 27 April, is taking place at a high security courtroom in the notorious Stammheim complex.
The defence team has repeatedly protested their clients’ treatment during proceedings, where the defendants are handcuffed and seated behind a glass barrier, preventing confidential communication with their lawyers.
The legal groups also challenged the court’s rejection of multiple applications by defence lawyers to hear expert witnesses.
MEE previously
reported
that the court refused to hear weapons expert Dr Shir Hever and international law expert Isabel Feichtner, who were presented by the defence team to give evidence regarding Elbit Systems’ role in
Israel’s genocide in Gaza
and Germany’s obligations under international law.
The organisations further rejected the use of Section 129 against the defendants, insisting that “the prosecution of specific acts of property damage must not be conflated with the criminalisation of a political protest movement”.
"A criminal trial must establish the relevant facts impartially," they urged. "It must not exclude politically inconvenient facts merely because they concern the conduct of a powerful arms manufacturer or the actions of a state in an ongoing armed conflict".

items.title: Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
items.content:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
Submitted by
Elis Gjevori
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 13:09
More than 1,680 interrogation torture complaints led to five criminal investigations, all closed without indictments
Palestinians released from Israeli prisons are examined by medics at the Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital in Deir el-Balah in the central Gaza Strip on 10 April 2025 (Eyad Baba/AFP)
Off
In 2021,
Israeli
police arrested a
Palestinian
man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.
He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.
The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.
Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.
He and his brother, who had also faced charges, eventually secured acquittals and their release.
Theirs was a rare case of acquittal within an Israeli justice system where torture, sexual assault, rape and inhuman treatment have become normalised, according to multiple reports from human rights organisations and the UN.
In its report, PCATI profiled 42 cases it had filed over the past decade on behalf of Palestinians who reported torture during Shin Bet interrogations.
In 33 of those cases, Palestinian detainees confessed under torture during or after questioning.
Israeli courts only recognised four of those confessions as false, despite interrogators using torture on the detainees.
The report describes how a confession extracted under duress can make its way into a criminal case.
UN: RSF used rape and sexual slavery as weapons of war in Sudan since 2023
Read More »
Israel does not examine the circumstances preceding a detainee’s confession when deciding whether they gave it “freely and voluntarily”, unlike other developed countries that explicitly ban torture and the use of any evidence obtained using it.
In one case, a journalist identified as M said she signed a police confession to stop the torture of her brother, whom interrogators had threatened.
She later pleaded guilty to a charge involving prohibited political activity.
In one case, official records showed that Shin Bet interrogated a Palestinian lawyer for about 552 hours over 27 and a half days, an average of 20 hours a day.
The lawyer, identified as TB, told an Israeli judge their client was in severe pain and could barely sleep. The court extended his detention.
The justice ministry unit that reviewed his complaint said interrogators had obtained the required authorisations to interrogate the man and declined to open a criminal investigation into the torture.
More than 1,680 complaints of abuse during interrogation reached the Israeli justice ministry’s oversight unit between 2001 and 2024, according to official figures obtained through freedom of information requests and cited in the report.
The unit recommended criminal investigations in five cases. Authorities closed all five files without an indictment.
Israel blacklisted
In May of this year, the United Nations added
Israel
to its blacklist for sexual violence in conflict zones.
The move follows multiple reports by human rights organisations and media outlets - including Middle East Eye - documenting allegations of rape and other forms of sexual violence by Israeli forces against
Palestinians
since October 2023.
New York Times article details brutal rape of Palestinians. Israel calls it 'blood libel'
Read More »
Israeli soldiers and prison guards have faced allegations of a wide range of abuses against Palestinian detainees since October 2023, including rape, torture, starvation and degrading treatment.
At least 100 prisoners have reportedly died in custody under these conditions, with nearly half dying in military detention and the remainder in facilities run by the IPS.
Dozens of testimonies from released detainees have detailed alleged mistreatment in Israeli custody.
In December, two Palestinians held in separate Israeli prisons
told MEE
they had suffered violent sexual assault.
One detainee said his jailers dragged him into a room where, for nearly an hour, they kicked, stamped on, insulted and raped him with an object while he wore a blindfold.
The other said trained military dogs raped him.
Last year, a UN
inquiry
accused Israel of using sexualised torture and rape as "a method of war... to destabilize, dominate, oppress and destroy the Palestinian people".
The Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem has
described
the Israeli prison system as a "network of torture camps" within which guards and soldiers subjected prisoners to the "repeated use of sexual violence", including "gang sexual violence and assault committed by a group of prison guards or soldiers".

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

items.title: More than a third of Muslim students experience Islamophobia at UK universities, report finds
items.content:
More than a third of Muslim students experience Islamophobia at UK universities, report finds
Submitted by
Areeb Ullah
on
Thu, 11/19/2026 - 17:12
Students surveyed by the Federation of Student Islamic Societies found that Muslim students from Russell Group universities faced more discrimination
Students hold a banner listing the names of people killed in Gaza during a pro-Palestine demonstration in London in October 2025 (Reuters)
Off
More than one in three Muslim students in the
UK
have experienced Islamophobia at university, with many facing abuse, threats and religious discrimination, according to a new report by the Federation of Student Islamic Societies (Fosis).
The report, titled
"Belonging in Question"
, found that 38 percent of Muslim students surveyed had experienced Islamophobia on campus, while 68 percent of those affected said they did not feel able to report what had happened to them.
Rahma Hegy, Fosis vice-president for student affairs, said Muslim students continued to make significant contributions to university life and wider British society, despite feeling unwelcome on campus.
"Many [students] tell us they do not feel they belong on the very campuses meant to include them," Hegy told Middle East Eye.
"They face discrimination, and too often they stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable."
Hegy said the lack of accountability was among the organisation's greatest concerns and urged universities, student unions and the government to act on it.
The findings are based on responses from 715 students across 63 higher education institutions in the UK, making it one of the largest recent surveys of Muslim students' experiences at British universities.
Students described a range of incidents, including being spat at, receiving death threats and having urine thrown at them while wearing the hijab.
Others reported being excluded from laboratory sessions after requesting time to attend Friday prayers, being told to remove their hijab before undertaking clinical placements, and being called terrorists while attending peaceful vigils.
'They face discrimination, and too often they stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable'
-
Rahma Hegy, Federation of Islamic Student Societies
The report found that Muslim women were more likely to experience Islamophobia than men, with 42 percent reporting discrimination compared with 34 percent of male respondents.
Students at Russell Group universities, which include some of the UK's most prestigious institutions, also reported higher levels of Islamophobia.
Forty-four percent of those interviewed said they had experienced discrimination, compared with 34 percent at other universities.
The findings also highlighted concerns about the impact of the political climate surrounding Palestine on Muslim students' ability to express themselves.
Three in five respondents said they felt afraid or intimidated to express their views on Palestine.
The report further found that 45 percent of students who had experienced Islamophobia said it had a moderate to severe impact on their mental health.
Fosis said the findings demonstrated a need for universities, students' unions and the government to take more decisive action to address anti-Muslim discrimination and protect students' rights.
The organisation is calling on universities to formally recognise Islamophobia, adopt a definition and introduce mandatory awareness training for university staff and student leaders.
It also wants universities to introduce a dedicated Islamophobia category in their reporting systems, improve the accessibility of prayer arrangements and ensure that academic timetables and clinical placements accommodate Muslim students' religious obligations.
'Mainstreaming far-right hatred'
The report urges institutions to hold staff and students accountable for Islamophobic behaviour, while calling on the government and higher education sector to protect freedom of expression and reduce what it describes as the securitisation of university campuses.
Among its recommendations is a review of the government's Prevent duty, which requires public institutions, including universities, to have due regard to preventing people from being drawn into terrorism.
UK school pays compensation to children threatened over Palestinian badges
Read More »
Former first minister of Scotland, Humza Yousaf, who wrote the foreword for the report, described the students' testimonies as being "as harrowing as they are infuriating".
"My family and I have been targeted with the most vile rape and death threats over the years, simply down to the faith we practice," said Yousaf.
"What we are witnessing, and what this report talks to, did not happen in a vacuum. I have warned time and again that too many in the political establishment were mainstreaming far-right hatred."
Yousaf called on universities to read the Fosis report as evidence rather than a complaint, arguing that the most "damning" finding is what happens after hostility occurs - where reporting barriers and weak institutional follow-through leave students without real change.
The Office for Students, which regulates higher education in England and monitors universities' compliance with the Prevent duty, had not responded to requests for comment at the time of publication.
Founded in 1963, Fosis is the national representative body for Muslim students in the UK and Ireland, bringing together more than 120 Islamic societies.
The report comes amid wider concerns about the treatment of pro-Palestinian activism in British universities, particularly following the outbreak of Israel's war on Gaza in October 2023.
Its findings raise questions about whether Muslim students can exercise their religious rights and freedom of political expression without facing discrimination or intimidation.

items.title: Israel kills security official and family in Gaza, as UN warns of 'real threat' to Palestinian existence
items.content:
Israel kills security official and family in Gaza, as UN warns of 'real threat' to Palestinian existence
Submitted by
Alex MacDonald
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 12:11
Killing of official in northern Gaza marks second deadly Israeli attack on security personnel in less than 24 hours and is condemned as an attempt to 'spread chaos' by the Interior Ministry
Mojahed Abu al-Ouf is consoled by his aunt at Al-Shifa Hospital as he bids farewell to his parents and two sisters after they were killed in an overnight Israeli air strike in Gaza City on 25 November 2026 (Omar al-Qattaa/AFP)
Off
A senior security official, his wife and his two daughters were killed in an
Israeli
air strike in
Gaza
overnight on Tuesday, as the UN warned of a "real threat" to
Palestinian
existence.
The attack on the apartment in Gaza City killed the director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, alongside his wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15.
It marked the second killing of a security official in Gaza in less than 24 hours, with the previous attack killing Naim Mohammed Abu Nahl, the director-general of the Internal Security Service.
The interior ministry slammed the attack on al-Awf as a "horrific massacre" and called for "urgent and genuine action to restrain the occupation from committing further crimes against innocent civilians" in the Gaza Strip.
"The Ministry of Interior and National Security condemns this heinous crime against security personnel and affirms that it comes within the context of ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society," it said in a statement.
Despite a so-called "ceasefire" established in October last year, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli attacks on Gaza since then, an average of four killed per day.
Threat to existence
UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned on Wednesday of a growing risk of further atrocity crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the
occupied West Bank
, urging all states to take immediate action to prevent them.
Turk cited inflammatory statements by senior Israeli officials advocating annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment, alongside increasingly widespread and systematic violations against Palestinians.
“Across society, the incitement to hatred and to perpetration of violations amounting to atrocity crimes - war crimes, crimes against humanity and even genocide - has been appalling,” he said in a statement.
Israel kills UN worker and two others across Gaza as attacks on Palestinians continue
Read More »
The UN rights chief said his office had repeatedly warned that Israel’s actions in Gaza posed a “real threat to the continued existence” of Palestinians as a group.
“Our warnings have not been heeded, and atrocity crimes continue to recur,” Turk added.
The vast majority of Gaza's population of 2.1 million now live in displaced in tents or makeshift shelters across the territory. At least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since October 2023, while the territory has been largely reduced to rubble.
Israel's military says it now controls more than 60 percent of the land.
On the day after the strike that killed a woman and her two teenage daughters alongside their father, Amnesty International said on Wednesday that Israel's attacks had inflicted disproportionate harm against Palestinian women and girls.
In a new 135-page
report
, the rights group documented the killing, maiming, forced displacement, unlawful detention and starvation of women and girls, as well as the deliberate denial of essential healthcare, including reproductive care, between October 2023 and October 2026.
“This new report sheds light on the profound gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide, providing new details about the brutal harms inflicted on women and girls that continue to devastate their lives and cause agonising suffering despite the so-called ceasefire,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general.

items.title: In Lebanon, the opening of a second airport reflects political shifts
items.content:
By Laila Bassam and Nazih Osseiran
KLEIAT AIRPORT, Lebanon, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Lebanon plans to open a second international airport next month to bring economic growth to the poorer north, in a project that underlines the diminished political sway of the Hezbollah group, which had long opposed it.
Kleiat Airport, located on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 km (12 miles) from the border crossing to Syria, will offer another gateway to Lebanon alongside Beirut international airport, where travel has been disrupted by wars between Israel and Hezbollah in recent years.

items.title: Israeli minister calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'
items.content:
Israeli minister calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'
The outgoing
Israeli
minister of heritage, Amichai Eliyahu, called
Palestinians
and Muslims "camel riders" and "barbarians" during a speech in parliament on Monday, amid escalating racist abuse against
Palestinian citizens of Israel
.
"Your education needs fixing. You need to be educated- not here in Israel, but everywhere in the world," Eliyahu said during a discussion on crime in Palestinian society in Israel.
"You destroyed the Twin Towers, you are destroying Europe, you make a mess everywhere you touch," said the minister, who previously suggested dropping an atomic bomb on the Gaza Strip.
"If you don't change, your children will die, and it's not because of us, it's because of you," added Eliyahu, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
Since Ben Gvir took over the ministry in late 2022, which oversees the police, crime in Palestinian society in Israel has skyrocketed. Palestinian leaders have accused Ben Gvir and the police force of allowing criminal organisations to operate unchecked.
Read more: Israeli minister calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'

items.title: Palestinians in Gaza face 'real threat' to their existence, says UN rights chief
items.content:
Palestinians in Gaza face 'real threat' to their existence, says UN rights chief
UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned on Wednesday of a growing risk of further atrocity crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, urging all states to take immediate action to prevent them.
Turk cited inflammatory statements by senior Israeli officials advocating annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment, alongside increasingly widespread and systematic violations against Palestinians.
“Across society, the incitement to hatred and to perpetration of violations amounting to atrocity crimes – war crimes, crimes against humanity and even genocide – has been appalling,” he said in a statement.
The UN rights chief said his office had repeatedly warned that Israel’s actions in Gaza posed a “real threat to the continued existence” of Palestinians as a group.
“Our warnings have not been heeded, and atrocity crimes continue to recur,” he added.

items.title: Amnesty says Palestinian women and girls bear crushing toll of Israel’s genocide
items.content:
Amnesty says Palestinian women and girls bear crushing toll of Israel’s genocide
Amnesty International said on Wednesday that Israel continues to inflict devastating harm on Palestinian women and girls in Gaza as part of its ongoing genocide, despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
In a new
135-page report
, the rights group documented the killing, maiming, forced displacement, unlawful detention and starvation of women and girls, as well as the deliberate denial of essential healthcare, including reproductive care, between October 2023 and October 2026.
“This new report sheds light on the profound gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide, providing new details about the brutal harms inflicted on women and girls that continue to devastate their lives and cause agonizing suffering despite the so-called ceasefire,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general.

items.content:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.
Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

items.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
items.content:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak
A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.
The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.

items.title: Israeli minister calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'
items.content:
Israeli minister calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'
Submitted by
Nadav Rapaport
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 10:41
Amichai Eliyahu’s racist remarks in parliament come amid a growing campaign of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel
Israeli Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu has previously said that using nuclear weapons in Gaza was an option (Screengrab/X)
Off
The outgoing
Israeli
minister of heritage, Amichai Eliyahu, called
Palestinians
and Muslims "camel riders" and "barbarians" during a speech in parliament on Monday, amid escalating racist abuse against
Palestinian citizens of Israel
.
"Your education needs fixing. You need to be educated- not here in Israel, but everywhere in the world," Eliyahu said during a discussion on crime in Palestinian society in Israel.
"You destroyed the Twin Towers, you are destroying Europe, you make a mess everywhere you touch," said the minister, who previously suggested dropping an atomic bomb on the Gaza Strip.
"If you don't change, your children will die, and it's not because of us, it's because of you," added Eliyahu, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
Since Ben Gvir took over the ministry in late 2022, which oversees the police, crime in Palestinian society in Israel has skyrocketed. Palestinian leaders have accused Ben Gvir and the police force of allowing criminal organisations to operate unchecked.
According to Haaretz, 204 Palestinians have been
murdered
in crime-related incidents in Israel since the beginning of 2026.
Most recently, an 11-year-old boy from occupied East Jerusalem was shot in the head on Saturday by a suspect who fled the scene.
Israeli police have also been accused of failing to solve murder cases affecting Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Since 2022, 166 Jewish and Palestinian women have been murdered, according to a
recent report
. It found that the rate of solved murder cases stood at 91 percent for Jewish victims, compared with just 26 percent for Palestinian victims.
Anti-Palestinian incitement
In his speech, Eliyahu addressed Palestinian MPs while attacking Muslims worldwide.
"Instead of being ignorant and uneducated camel riders, learn from Jewish, western morality," he told them.
"Instead of murdering one another, slaughtering other peoples, carrying out suicide attacks, stand on your feet and fight," he added, arguing that if Palestinians wanted to end the violence on their streets, they needed "to educate according to the values of the Torah of Israel, of the western world".
According to Israeli news outlet Ynet,
nine of the 11 Knesset members
with PhDs belong to the Palestinian-led Joint List and Ra'am parties. Neither of the other two belong to Eliyahu's Otzma Yehudit party.
'We are witnessing a wild and unrestrained campaign of incitement against our community'
- Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List
Eliyahu's remarks come amid a violent campaign of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies since Ra'am and the Joint List won an unprecedented 19 Knesset seats in last month's elections.
Netanyahu and his far-right allies have accused the Palestinian-led parties of being "supporters of terrorism".
On Tuesday, the Israeli Knesset's legal adviser, Sagit Afik, said lawmakers were permitted to call a colleague a "terror supporter".
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, addressed the mounting racist attacks against Palestinian citizens of Israel on Monday,
saying
: "We are witnessing a wild and unrestrained campaign of incitement against our community."
Jabareen accused Netanyahu of fuelling the incitement and called on Jewish opposition leaders to form a government reliant on the support of the Palestinian-led parties.

items.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
items.content:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views
James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.
Chambers’s case is the
first known instance
of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.
Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

items.content:
By Joshua McElwee
VATICAN CITY, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Pope Leo on Wednesday sharply criticised the failure of UN climate talks over the weekend, calling the outcome "troubling" and urging world leaders to step up efforts to combat climate change.
"In the face of the growing frequency of extreme environmental events linked to the climate crisis, it is troubling that COP 31 ended without the international community adopting clear commitments to address it seriously and responsibly," the pope told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter's Square.

CAIRO, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Israel's military killed a senior Hamas security official as well as his wife and two children with an airstrike on their Gaza Strip apartment early on Wednesday, Gaza's Hamas-run Interior Ministry and medics said.
The airstrike that killed Mohammad Abuelouf, a Hamas colonel who headed the militants' internal security service in northern Gaza, and his family was the second Israeli attack to kill a senior Hamas security official in the past 24 hours.
